paragraphs.text: Rougui, cassia in Chinese, is a [Wuyi cultivar](yancha:rougui) that dates from the Qing dynasty and is now one of the most widely planted teas in the range. It is made as [rock tea](yancha:definition), with the leaf twisted into long, thin strips rather than rolled into balls.

The leaf comes from the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), on the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi. The mountains hold in warm air from the sea, so rain is heavy and fog is common, and the bushes grow in [thin, stony soil](wuyi-mountains:nature) on ledges and between rocks, where the ground drains fast. The label names no zone, so it does not say how close to the [true rock core](wuyi-mountains:zones) this tea grew.

This lot was given a heavy [charcoal roast](yancha:making) in stages over several sessions. That is how the craft works: rounds over charcoal with rests of weeks or months between them, rather than one pass, so the tea dries and keeps.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
